body_markdown:
All cars need maintenance. Well, the ones you expect to continue operating efficiently and effectively do, anyway. The most efficient and effective cars in the world might just be[Formula 1](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/kinardi-line/kinardi-line-9-what-monster-trucks-could-teach-formula-1/) race cars. Some will disagree, but the amount of time and effort spent keeping each and every part of these top-tier machines in tip-top shape will likely prove them wrong. When the cars are nearly completely rebuilt and inspected between every race, it’s easy to see the need for some crazy organization and efficiency.


This look inside the life of a Formula 1 chassis comes[via Cadillac](https://youtu.be/WqeAHMTOvUY?si=aQDmTMWqOPRzs3Uv) and is a nice way to see into the program and get a glimpse of the complexity that makes spinning up a new team in such high-level motorsport so difficult.


The whole process starts when the car gets back to team headquarters after a race. Each part is stripped down as much as possible before being subjected to careful inspection. How careful? Well, the carbon fiber composites that comprise so much of an F1 car these days get testing ultrasonically for cracks or inclusions that might propagate while the car is on track. Each piece is documented with a serial number, which allows engineers to log the events it has traveled to, how many times it has been assembled, seen track time, or even crashed.


Each individual part is tested carefully.

So many bins, so many parts.

From there it becomes a game of the engineers piecing together the setup they feel will be best for[a given track](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/rwanda-african-grand-prix-track-date/) and sending a build sheet of sorts over to another internal team that decides which of the parts available will be used to assemble the car and which parts might travel as spares. All of those are documented and cataloged before going into shipping containers. It’s like meal prepping, but for a car.


Is this a level of care that needs to be applied to every car that might see track time? Likely not, as most motorsports cars do not run as close to the edge of failure as an F1 car does. Or, at least we hope so. The idea of thorough inspections is a good one, but blowing the car fully apart between events might be overkill for a Spec Miata or a street car that sees a few autocrosses a year. Regardless, a quick look inside the massive, high-dollar operations of F1 is always entertaining.


The packing and un-packing of all the parts after each event can take days.
